newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin sees NATO deal with Clinton, says now fit.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin sees NATO deal with Clinton, says now fit.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, declaring himself fighting fit again on Russia's annual celebration of military might, hit out at NATO's expansion plans and said he expected Bill Clinton to compromise at a summit next month.

"We are firm in our position. We are opposed to NATO enlargement. Our task now is to stall it as long as possible and not allow the renewal of confrontation," Yeltsin said after a short ceremony marking Russia's Defenders of the Fatherland Day.

"We have agreed to look for a compromise and I think we will find this compromise at the summit we are holding with President Clinton on March 20-21 in Helsinki," he told reporters on his first public appearance since he caught pneumonia at New Year.
On Friday, Yeltsin, 66, discussed plans for the summit with U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright. Albright said she made "important progress" but much work was still needed.
Journalists who spoke to Yeltsin said the president was bright and alert. He walked steadily if slowly during the 20-minute wreath-laying ceremony at the Kremlin war memorial.

"I have fully recovered now. I just have to gain some strength," he said. He was feeling stronger after losing 26 kg (57 pounds) since the November heart bypass surgery which has kept him on the sidelines since his re-election last July.
Asked about parliament's attempts to remove him on health grounds, he growled: "I am a fighter and I remain a fighter. They shouldn't attack me too hard because I can hit back."

The Helsinki summit -- switched from the United States because of Yeltsin's health problems -- may emerge as the finale of an elaborate diplomatic dance in which western officials are trying to overcome Moscow's bitter opposition to plans to allow former Soviet-bloc states in eastern Europe to join NATO.

"Knowing that pure Yeltsin style of solving problems in one go and in the most unexpected ways, this summit could get rid of the bitterest issues dividing Moscow and Washington," the liberal Nezavisimaya Gazeta newspaper wrote at the weekend.

Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov was due to meet NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana later on Sunday for a second round of detailed talks as part of the buildup to a July summit in Madrid where NATO hopes to settle the expansion issue.
Western diplomats said Solana wanted to see how far Moscow was prepared to compromise following several NATO concessions.

It has offered to revise a 1990 treaty on the deployment of conventional forces and give Russia a say in NATO. The West has pledged not to base nuclear arms in new member states. The Czech Republic, Poland and Hungary are the favourites for early entry.

Moscow, which sees NATO expansion as a threat and a domestic political embarrassment, has been holding out for a legally binding treaty laying down relations between NATO and Russia -- something Washington has not been prepared to countenance.
The government newspaper "Rossiiskaya Gazeta" conceded in a weekend editorial that Moscow could not veto NATO's expansion.

"Alas, the train has left and Russia is in no condition to give it the red light," commentator Vladimir Lapsky wrote. "The Russian government understands that and is basing its policy on finding an optimal accord with the West on the speed of this train, on what stops it makes and, especially, on its cargo."
The government needs no reminding of the importance of being seen by voters to be defending Russia's interests.

Thousands of communists and nationalist marched through Moscow on Sunday under red banners accusing Yeltsin of wrecking the Soviet superpower and undermining the army. The Defence Ministry newspaper "Krasnaya Zvyeda" said the military was suffering badly from unpaid wages and deteriorating equipment.

Weekend media also gave prominence to Friday's visit by Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin to the nuclear missile command. He warned European defence planners not to overlook Moscow's still mighty atomic potential.
